title: The fish sign
hook: a fish, two curved lines: in Greek, its letters spell the initials of Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus, and your line was awake, creative, glad to be in a body. What did you do on purpose, and what did it wake up in you? Day seven hundred sixty-one.
screen: `AWAKE, CREATIVE, GLAD TO BE IN A BODY.`

segments.voice: Two curved lines, crossing at one end. That's all it takes. A child can draw it in the sand. It turns up on the backs of cars, on necklaces, on bakery signs and business cards. It tells you, roughly, that somebody here is a Christian. But why a fish? It isn't a cross. It isn't a lamb or a dove. It's lunch. And the answer turns out to be a word puzzle, hidden in plain sight, in Greek.

The Greek word for fish is ichthys. Five letters: iota, chi, theta, upsilon, sigma. Take each letter as the first letter of a word, and you get a creed. Iesous: Jesus. Christos: Christ. Theou: of God. Huios: Son. Soter: Savior. Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior. Augustine, writing about it in the City of God, spells out the five Greek words and says that when you join their first letters you get ichthys, fish, and that Christ is understood in the word. Then he adds a picture: Christ could live without sin in the deep waters of this mortal life, the way a fish lives in the depths. Earlier still, a North African writer named Tertullian makes the fish a picture of baptism. In his book on baptism he calls Christians little fishes, born in water, following our Ichthys, Jesus Christ. So the fish is a word game, and also a picture of baptism. And it swims through the Gospels too. Jesus calls fishermen: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." He feeds crowds with loaves and fishes. After the resurrection, in John's Gospel, he cooks fish on a beach for his friends. Now, the secret part. Tradition says early Christians scratched the fish on walls and tombs. And there's a story told today: in times of danger, one stranger would draw one curve in the dust, and if the other drew the second curve, they knew they were safe together. It's a good story. The ancient writers quoted here don't tell it. What they do show is a sign whose meaning was explained openly, in books anyone could read. A secret, maybe, mostly in the way a family's private joke is secret. You have to be inside to get it.

Here's the practice: draw the fish. With a finger on the table, a pen on a scrap of paper, or just in the air. One curve. Then the other, crossing at the tail. Then trace it slowly, again and again, and let the five words go by with it if you like: Jesus. Christ. God's. Son. Savior. If you pray, those five words can be your prayer, nothing added. If you don't, just keep tracing, and notice how small a thing can carry a whole meaning. The bell holds the time.
Ichthys. Greek for fish. Its five letters begin five words: Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior.
Your line: the secret sign. Today, notice one small sign that tells you something to people who know it: a fish, a cross, a word, a habit. Ask what it says. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians use the fish symbol on jewelry, cars, signs and church art as a quiet sign of faith, and some teach children the five Greek words behind it.
